exam: A 7‑year‑old presents with behavioural change and myoclonus 8 years after measles – what is the most likely diagnosis and why? — SSPE; delayed onset, characteristic EEG, high CSF measles IgG.
How would you confirm SSPE if MRI is unavailable? — Perform EEG for periodic complexes and CSF measles antibody ratio.
What preventive strategy would you advise the community to eliminate SSPE? — Achieve > 95 % measles vaccination coverage with two doses.
Why is ribavirin rarely used in this setting? — High cost, need for monitoring, and limited evidence of survival benefit.
A patient with SSPE develops worsening seizures; which drug class should you add and why? — Add a broad‑spectrum antiepileptic such as valproate to control myoclonus and prevent status epilepticus.

Differentiate SSPE from acute measles encephalitis in terms of onset and investigations. — SSPE: years after infection, no fever, EEG periodic complexes; Encephalitis: days after rash, fever, CSF pleocytosis.
What are the red‑flag signs that require urgent referral? — Rapid loss of consciousness, new focal deficits, respiratory compromise.
Explain why a high CSF‑serum measles IgG ratio is diagnostic. — Indicates intrathecal synthesis of antibodies, a hallmark of persistent CNS infection.
ai.title: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: SSPE is a rare, fatal, delayed complication of measles caused by persistent defective measles virus in the brain. It presents years after infection with progressive neurodegeneration. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria and EEG/CSF findings; treatment is supportive.

b: Incidence highest in low‑resource settings with poor measles vaccination coverage.
Fatal within 1‑3 years of symptom onset if untreated.
sections.p: SSPE occurs 5‑15 years after a measles infection, most often in children infected before age 2. The virus remains in the CNS as an altered, replication‑defective strain that triggers chronic inflammation and neuronal loss.

b: Defective virus persists in neurons and glia.
Triggers chronic immune activation and demyelination.
sections.p: Measles virus (Paramyxoviridae, genus Morbillivirus) is an enveloped, negative‑sense RNA virus. In SSPE the virus has mutations in the matrix (M) and fusion (F) genes, preventing full virion assembly but allowing spread via cell‑to‑cell fusion (syncytia).

b: Primary prevention: measles vaccination (MCV1 at 9 months, MCV2 at 12‑15 months).
No secondary prophylaxis for contacts of SSPE patients.
sections.p: Measles spreads by respiratory droplets; after acute infection the virus is cleared from most tissues but can hide in the CNS. No person‑to‑person transmission of SSPE occurs.

b: Stage I: personality change, insomnia, seizures.
Stage II: worsening myoclonus, visual disturbances.
Stage III: severe motor disability, aphasia.
sections.p: SSPE presents with a characteristic triad: behavioral change, myoclonus, and progressive cognitive decline. Staging (Jabbour) helps gauge severity:
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EEG, CSF, and, where available, measles antibody titres.

t.b: Does the patient have periodic high‑voltage slow wave complexes? → Presence of stereotyped 1‑2 Hz bursts strongly supports SSPE.
Is measles antibody markedly elevated in CSF compared with serum? → Ratio > 1.5 is diagnostic of SSPE.
Are there hyperintense white‑matter lesions on T2/FLAIR? → Helps exclude other demyelinating diseases; lesions are often diffuse but non‑specific.

b: Isoprinosine (inosine pranobex) – enhances cellular immunity; used when available.
Ribavirin – oral or intraventricular; limited by toxicity and cost.
Supportive care: physiotherapy, nutrition, seizure control.
sections.p: No cure exists; therapy aims to slow progression and manage symptoms. Antivirals and immune modulators are used where resources permit.

t.b: Are enzymes elevated before starting isoprinosine or ribavirin? → Detects hepatic risk; if unavailable, monitor clinically for jaundice.

b: Link delayed onset (years) to prior measles infection, especially before age 2.
Describe the characteristic EEG pattern (periodic high‑voltage slow waves).
State why measles vaccination is the only proven preventive measure.
Explain why ribavirin is rarely used in low‑resource settings (cost, toxicity).
Differentiate SSPE from acute encephalitis (rapid onset, fever) and from progressive neurodegenerative disorders.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid deterioration in consciousness, new seizures, or respiratory failure – requires urgent transfer to a higher‑level facility.
